headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Postpartum Care
headings.content: The postpartum period, or puerperium, begins immediately after the delivery of the placenta and extends for six weeks. This phase marks a critical transition where the mother's body undergoes profound anatomical and physiological adaptations to return to the pre-pregnant state. Postpartum care encompasses structured medical, nursing, and emotional support provided to the mother and newborn during these crucial weeks. In Nigerian clinical practice, ensuring comprehensive care during this window significantly reduces maternal morbidity and mortality associated with postpartum hemorrhage and sepsis.

headings.title: Immediate Postpartum Physiological Changes and Involution
headings.content:
Uterine involution is the rapid reduction in the size of the uterus following childbirth. Immediately after placental delivery, the fundus should feel firm, globular, and sit roughly at or one centimeter below the umbilicus. Over the next two weeks, the uterus descends progressively into the pelvic cavity until it is no longer palpable abdominally. Lochia evolves through three distinct stages:

- **Lochia rubra**: Bright red discharge lasting from day one to day three, consisting primarily of blood, decidual tissue, and trophoblastic debris.
- **Lochia serosa**: Pinkish-brown discharge appearing from day four to day ten, containing serous fluid, leukocytes, and mucus.
- **Lochia alba**: Yellowish-white discharge persisting from week two to week six, composed mostly of leukocytes, epithelial cells, and cholesterol.

headings.title: Comprehensive Maternal Assessment in the Puerperium
headings.content: Systematic nursing assessment during the puerperium uses the standard mnemonic BUBBLE-EE, which directs evaluation of the breasts, uterus, bladder, bowel, lochia, episiotomy/perineum, extremities, and emotional state. Vital signs require strict monitoring, as a rising pulse or dropping blood pressure can be the earliest indicator of concealed postpartum hemorrhage. Assessment of the perineum must include checking for excessive edema, hematoma formation, or localized infection around repair sites.

headings.title: Routine Postpartum Nursing Interventions and Comfort Measures
headings.content: Managing post-delivery discomfort requires targeted, practical nursing interventions. Perineal pain from episiotomies or lacerations responds well to cold packs during the first twenty-four hours to reduce edema, followed by Sitz baths to promote healing and comfort. Promoting early ambulation prevents thromboembolic events, provided vital signs have stabilized. Nurses must also monitor bladder elimination closely; postpartum urinary retention caused by regional anesthesia or perineal trauma can lead to uterine atony and subsequent hemorrhage.

headings.title: Nutrition, Hygiene, and Self-Care Education
headings.content: Recovery demands increased nutritional intake, particularly for lactating mothers who require an extra daily caloric intake along with adequate protein, calcium, and iron supplementation to replenish stores lost during childbirth and prevent anemia. Perineal hygiene education is vital; mothers should learn to clean the perineum from front to back using clean water after every voiding or defecation to prevent ascending urinary tract infections. Adequate hydration and high-fiber diets are equally emphasized to manage common postpartum constipation.

headings.title: Postpartum Psychological Adjustment and Mental Health Screening
headings.content: Emotional vulnerability is high following childbirth due to sudden hormonal drops, sleep deprivation, and the demands of newborn care. While transient 'baby blues' characterized by mild tearfulness and mood lability resolve independently within two weeks, persistent symptoms require active intervention. Nurses must screen for postpartum depression using tools like the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Recognizing severe manifestations such as postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that demands immediate referral to prevent harm to the mother or infant.

headings.title: Identification and Management of Postpartum Complications
headings.content: Early recognition of pathological deviations saves lives during the puerperium. Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as blood loss exceeding 500 mL following vaginal delivery or 1000 mL following a cesarean section, frequently caused by uterine atony. Puerperal sepsis presents with persistent fever, foul-smelling lochia, and lower abdominal pain. Thromboembolic complications demand vigilance for signs of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, which remain significant causes of maternal mortality.

headings.title: Neonatal Transition Support and Breastfeeding Guidance
headings.content: Supporting the neonate during the immediate transition involves maintaining thermal regulation, clearing airways gently, and initiating early skin-to-skin contact. Exclusive breastfeeding should begin within the first hour of life, maximizing the benefits of colostrum. Nurses must assess infant latch technique regularly to prevent maternal complications like sore nipples and engorgement while ensuring the infant receives adequate nutrition evidenced by frequent wet diapers and steady weight gain.

headings.title: Family Planning and Postpartum Discharge Counseling
headings.content: Discussing family planning is an essential component of postpartum discharge counseling before the mother leaves the healthcare facility. Ovulation can return before the first postpartum menses, making contraceptive education imperative during the early puerperium. Progestin-only methods, barrier methods, and intrauterine devices can be discussed based on individual client preferences and lactation status. Discharge education must also reinforce danger signs that necessitate immediate return to the hospital, including heavy vaginal bleeding, severe headaches, and chest pain.
